summary: Discovery call for on-prem air-gapped deployment. Discussed differences between Hosted/Dedicated/Private and constraints around hardware, offline updates, and security review process. Agreed to pilot a benchmark in their lab and share security pack.
questions: How do offline updates work for model weights and runtime?
Can Redwood integrate with our HSM (YubiHSM/FortiHSM)?
What telemetry, if any, leaves the air-gapped environment?
What are the recommended GPU configs for 8k token models?
transcription:
Meeting header: 2026-02-05 15:00 PST | Duration 48m
Attendees: Jason Lee, Priya Nair, Marta Gomez (Redwood) — Dr. Elena Márquez, Mark Benson, Aisha Khan, Tom Rivers (Cobalt Space)

Summary (auto): Quick discovery to validate fit for on-prem, air-gapped deployment; high-security org.

[00:00] Jason Lee: Hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro — I'm Jason, AE on the account, with Priya and Marta from solutions and infra. Elena, want to kick off with a bit of context on Cobalt's constraints?
[00:17] Dr. Elena Márquez: Yeah thanks Jason. We're looking at LLM inference for internal ops automation and anomaly detection, but we have to be fully air-gapped, no external egress. All crypto keys live in our HSM, and any software must pass supply-chain review. So, the main question is can Redwood run entirely inside our network, offline, and how do updates happen?
[00:34] Priya Nair: Totally. We support Redwood Private which is the on-prem package; it can be deployed in an air-gapped environment. Updates are designed to be offline — we provide artifacts that you can pull into your environment and apply via an offline bundle. There is a signed bundle approach, it's similar to our on-prem process we've done for other defense / health customers.
[00:53] Mark Benson: When you say signed bundle, can we verify with our HSM? We need hardware-rooted attestation and signatures gone through our HSM chain.
[01:06] Marta Gomez: Yes, the package is signed and we can provide a signature verification step. In many installs customers verify the signature using their HSM; we can work with your security team on the fingerprinting process. There might be a slight manual step for the first install.
[01:22] Aisha Khan: What about telemetry? We cannot have any telemetry phoning home.
[01:28] Priya Nair: By default the Private on-prem build can be configured with telemetry disabled. There are toggle flags at install time; for air-gapped customers we typically ship with telemetry off and use offline log bundles for support. Support would need a deliberate log export.
[01:46] Tom Rivers: Great. Hardware — do you have a recommended GPU profile? We're currently looking at a mix of A100 40GB and some older V100s in our lab. We plan to run smaller batches but need 8k token support for a couple internal models.
[02:02] Priya Nair: For 8k token context, A100 40GB is preferred; for 8k we recommend at least 40GB memory per worker, ideally 80GB for larger batch concurrency. V100s will work with heavy sharding and reduced batch sizes, but latency and throughput will be impacted. We also have quantized runtime builds that reduce GPU memory but require validation for quality.
[02:22] Dr. Elena Márquez: What about KV cache persistence? Our workload reuses prefixes a lot, so we want to ensure warm-cache performance across restarts.
[02:32] Marta Gomez: We have KV cache persistence options in Private — you can mount a local SSD-backed KV store and configure checkpointing frequency. In air-gapped installs customers usually set up periodic snapshot exports to internal secure storage.
[02:44] Mark Benson: On the compliance side, do you provide SBOM and third-party library lists? Our supply chain team will need that.
[02:52] Jason Lee: Yes, we produce SBOMs and dependency manifests; we'll add those to the security pack. We'll include known CVE mappings and recommended patch cadence.
[03:04] Aisha Khan: For keys, can Redwood integrate with our HSM? We're using YubiHSM for both signing and key storage.
[03:12] Priya Nair: We integrate with KMS/HSM providers via KMIP or PKCS11 depending on the HSM. We've done YubiHSM integrations before; there may be a connector step on your side. For true offline operations the HSM stays on-prem and the runtime fetches keys locally — no keys leave the environment.
[03:34] Tom Rivers: Update process details — if there's a model update, like new weights, what's the flow?
[03:41] Marta Gomez: The typical flow: we produce a signed model artifact and a runtime bundle. You ingest the signed artifacts into your private repo, verify signatures with your HSM, then trigger the deploy in your cluster. If you want, Redwood can provide an offline validation suite that runs locally and checks runtime compatibility.
[03:58] Dr. Elena Márquez: How long does it usually take to get an offline bundle patched and ready? We have a long change window and need to coordinate maintenance nights.
[04:06] Priya Nair: It depends on the change — a security patch to runtime usually can be produced within 2-4 business days for critical fixes; model weight updates are quicker but still require signed artifacts and a validation pass. For larger feature releases we schedule quarterly offline bundles.
[04:22] Mark Benson: Network isolation — we have strict egress rules and our build system is entirely internal. Do you require any outbound connections for license checks?
[04:32] Jason Lee: No, for Private on-prem we can operate without outbound license checks. The license is delivered as an offline license file that your infra team installs. We offer optional heartbeat for Dedicated/Hosted only — not for air-gapped Private.
[04:46] Aisha Khan: Ok, what about logging and audit trails — we need tamper-evident logs and integration with our SIEM (Splunk).
[04:55] Marta Gomez: The on-prem agent supports structured audit logs and can forward to local syslog or Splunk HEC endpoints inside your network. Logs can be signed and we can provide guidance on log retention and rotation to meet tamper-evidence requirements.
[05:10] Tom Rivers: Does Redwood provide a build artifact signature verification tool or do we need to build that?
[05:17] Priya Nair: We provide a signature verification CLI as part of the offline bundle. It uses public-key signatures, and customers often wrap it in their own attestation workflow that uses HSM-signed verification.
[05:30] Dr. Elena Márquez: We're also worried about model provenance and evaluation. Can you provide eval harnesses so we can reproduce your benchmark numbers locally during the pilot?
[05:39] Jason Lee: Absolutely — we can share an eval harness and the dataset subset used for the benchmark. For the pilot we'll coordinate which prompts/metrics matter to you.
[05:49] Mark Benson: On the business model: is Private on-prem a license + support fee? What's typical for pilot pricing?
[05:58] Jason Lee: Yes, on-prem typically is a platform license plus a support contract. For pilots we often do a time-limited license or reduced pilot pricing — we'll include options in the quote. For larger enterprise you'd look at annual licensing and optional premium SLAs.
[06:12] Aisha Khan: Any known gotchas with air-gapped installs?
[06:16] Marta Gomez: Biggest issues are patch management windows and hardware driver compatibility (NVIDIA driver versions, CUDA). Another common snag is NICs and MTU settings when customers try to do RDMA or multi-host KV cache. We provide a hardware checklist to minimize surprises.
[06:33] Tom Rivers: We use a private PCIe switch topology for our GPUs; do you have examples where that was supported?
[06:40] Priya Nair: Yes, we've deployed into similar topologies. We'll need the exact network/cross-host fabric details to confirm. Some RDMA setups need kernel modules present; our deploy engineer will review.
[06:55] Dr. Elena Márquez: About model variants and fallbacks — suppose you want to do canary rollouts of new quantized variants, can we keep the policy local?
[07:05] Marta Gomez: Policies are fully configurable in the Private control plane; you can do canary, A/B, or pin specific model versions per route. Because it's on-prem, those rollouts only touch your environment.
[07:16] Mark Benson: And telemetry again — assume it's off. If we need Redwood to run a remote debug session, what's the path?
[07:24] Jason Lee: We do support an out-of-band debug process where you create a support bundle and share it via secure transfer (SFTP or internal ticketing). There's no automatic remote access.
[07:34] Aisha Khan: Who owns the keys for model encryption at rest?
[07:38] Priya Nair: You own the keys; we support KMS/HSM integration. Model weights at rest can be encrypted with keys you manage in your HSM.
[07:47] Tom Rivers: Performance benchmarks — can Redwood run local performance tests or do you want us to run them?
[07:54] Marta Gomez: We can run benchmark scripts locally during the pilot. Typically Priya's team provides a harness and we coordinate with your infra to run it against your sample workload. We'll capture latency p95/p99 and throughput numbers.
[08:06] Jason Lee: Are there any contractual requirements from your side like FedRAMP, ITAR, or export controls?
[08:13] Dr. Elena Márquez: We're not ITAR, but we do have DoD-adjacent contracts and strict export controls on certain data sets. We'll need to confirm with legal.
[08:22] Mark Benson: Timeline — we're hoping to have a pilot inside Q2. Is that doable?
[08:27] Jason Lee: Yes Q2 pilot is reasonable. We'll get you a statement of work and pilot plan.
[08:33] Priya Nair: For the pilot we'll want: (1) list of GPU machines, (2) a test dataset sample (sanitized), (3) a maintenance window for install, and (4) a point of contact for security.
[08:45] Tom Rivers: We'll confirm that. Also curious about support SLAs — if something breaks in pilot how quickly can you respond on-site or remote?
[08:53] Jason Lee: Pilot support is remote; for enterprise support we offer on-call 24/7 and optional on-site engagements under a separate SOW. We'll include SLA tiers in the quote.
[09:05] Dr. Elena Márquez: What about integration with our internal model registry? We use an internal artifact repo (Artifactory) for weights and SHA-based addressing.
[09:15] Marta Gomez: We can point the Private runtime to a local artifact repo and use checksums to fetch models. The recommended pattern is to mirror our signed artifacts into your Artifactory and let your CI/CD handle promotion across environments.
[09:29] Mark Benson: Any special licensing for multi-region air-gapped sites? We have two labs in different countries.
[09:36] Jason Lee: Licensing is typically per deployment cluster. We can offer multi-site licensing or a seat-based model; will include options. Regional compliance may affect the support contract.
[09:48] Aisha Khan: Ok, slightly random: what does Redwood require from our IDS/IPS for the deploy? Any ports or services we need to allow at install?
[09:57] Priya Nair: For air-gapped installs minimal ports are required internally — kube API, image registry (internal), and optional metrics endpoints. We'll send a firewall/ports checklist. There's no outbound egress needed.
[10:10] Tom Rivers: On metrics, can we forward Prometheus metrics locally?
[10:15] Marta Gomez: Yes, we expose Prometheus metrics and can integrate with your internal monitoring stack.
[10:20] [--- brief cross talk and short pause while someone pulls up a doc ---]
[10:40] Dr. Elena Márquez: I have one last question about attestation during deploy: can you provide reproducible build artifacts so we can do deterministic verification?
[10:48] Jason Lee: We can provide reproducible build hashes and the SBOM. Deterministic builds are part of the supply-chain documentation, we'll include what we can.
[10:57] Mark Benson: Ok great. Let's outline next steps.
[11:01] Jason Lee: Recap: we'll send security package (SBOM, SOC2 excerpt, signature verification tool), hardware checklist, and a draft pilot SOW + pricing. Priya will own the benchmark plan. We'll target a 2-hour workshop next week to scope the pilot and run the initial benchmark in your lab.
[11:20] Dr. Elena Márquez: Sounds good. Please HOLD telemetry off by default in the pilot.
[11:25] Jason Lee: Noted. We'll ensure telemetry disabled.
[11:28] Aisha Khan: And include a clear procedure for emergency patches and offline distribution.
[11:33] Priya Nair: We'll outline patch cadence and emergency process in the pilot SOW.
[11:38] Tom Rivers: I'll gather the GPU inventory and NIC details and send to Jason/Tom? (laughs) — send to Jason, sorry.
[11:46] Jason Lee: Thanks Tom. We'll follow up on scheduling. Appreciate the time everyone.
[11:50] Dr. Elena Márquez: Thanks all.

Notes: transcript timestamps are approximate; some segments mildly garbled as auto-transcript.
end_notes: Call ended with clear next steps: security pack, hardware checklist, pilot SOW, schedule benchmark workshop. Agreed telemetry off and HSM integration. Follow-up items assigned.
